en.title: Greeting and introducing yourself
en.summary: How to say hello, give your name and say where you are from, and the grammar of the verb be.

paragraphs: When you meet someone in English, you say hello, give your name and often say where you are from. These few sentences use the most important verb in the language, the verb be. In this lesson you will read a short conversation and then see how the grammar works.
Anna and Tom meet on the first day of an English course in London.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.text: Hello! My name is Anna. What's your name?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Hi, Anna. I'm Tom. Nice to meet you.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.text: Nice to meet you, too. Where are you from?

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.text: I'm from Poland, but I live in London now.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.text: Yes, I am. I study English here. Are you a student, too?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: No, I'm not. I'm a teacher.

paragraphs: In a formal situation, such as a business meeting, people say **Good morning. How do you do?** or **Pleased to meet you.** The answer to How do you do? is the same words: **How do you do?**

**1. The verb be changes with the subject.** In the conversation you read I'm, you are, My name is. In speaking, people nearly always use the short forms. See Introduction to Grammar: Present tense, being and having.

paragraphs: **2. A question with be puts the verb first.** The statement **You are a student** becomes the question **Are you a student?** A short answer repeats the verb: **Yes, I am.** or **No, I'm not.** A positive short answer is never shortened, so we do not say Yes, I'm. See Introduction to Grammar: Negation and questions.

items: English has only one word for you. You use it with friends, teachers and strangers. Politeness comes from words such as please, from titles such as Mr or Ms, and from your tone.
After the word from you name a place: **from Canada**, **from London**.
**How are you?** is a greeting as much as a question. The usual answer is **Fine, thanks. And you?**, even on a bad day.

paragraphs: In the United Kingdom and the United States people often shake hands when they meet for the first time in a formal situation. Friends usually just say hello. In many English-speaking countries people start using first names quickly, even at work.
